title: Etta and the Festival Whistles
markdown:
The forest was buzzing, and little Etta the cave explorer knew why. Her magnifying glass practically vibrated. Happy feet tap-tapped the floor. The annual Forest Festival was just around the corner: fun, decorations that twinkled. This year Etta, her best bat-friend Brim, and kind Ranger Jo had an important job: cheerful chimes for the cavalcade, sounding as happy as sunshine through leaves.

Etta held a little hollow reed, no thicker than her finger. “Let’s try this one, Brim!” Cheeks puffed. She blew with all her might.

Squeeeeeeak! So high the leaves shivered. Brim’s sensitive ears flapped. Tiny leathery paws over them.

“Oh, my goodness, my ears!” Voice wobbly, whiskers frantic, a little hop. “A very, very, very high sound, Etta! A tickle in my ear-flaps!”

Ranger Jo offered a smooth round piece of wood, like a little drum with a hole. Etta blew. Pfffft. Quiet as a sleepy dormouse sigh.

“Too quiet.” Brow like a tiny worried cloud. Shoulders sagged. “The parade needs to sound happy and loud, so everyone can hear us coming! But not so squeaky it hurts Brim’s ears!”

They tried and tried. They tried different reeds, some thin and wispy, others fat and sturdy. They tried hollowed-out sticks, smooth pebbles with holes, and even little dried gourds that rattled when they shook them. Some whistles were too high, making Brim hop with surprise. Some were too soft, making them lean in to hear. And some just made a funny wheezing puff that wasn’t much of a whistle at all. The festival was only two days away, and Etta’s shoulders drooped like wilting wildflowers after a long hot day.

Ranger Jo’s voice was a stream over stones. “Sometimes the answer is hiding, like a shy ladybug under a leaf.”

Brim, who had been looping above for a better view, zipped down onto a mossy branch, head tilted.

“Etta! Ranger Jo! I was flying past the Whispering Caves near the Whispering Falls. Some caves echo with a deep rumble. Others with a tiny tinkle.”

Etta’s eyes lit like fireflies. “Yes! The Big Echo Cave sounds like a giant’s gentle grumble. The Tiny Twinkle Cave like little fairy bells!”

“Exactly! The sounds are different! Some deep, some high!”

Etta ran with her magnifying glass to discarded reeds and pebbles by an empty burrow. A very thin short reed, no thicker than a worm. Blow. Squeeee! “Too high, like before.” A thicker longer reed, like a sturdy straw. Blow. Tooooooot! Deeper, warmer, a friendly greeting.

Tiny reed, high. Bigger reed, low.

“Look!” Two reeds held up. “This tiny reed makes a tiny high sound! This bigger reed makes a bigger, lower sound!” Two pebbles tapped: tink, tink, light. Two larger stones: thump, thump, heavier, a vibration in the chest.

“It’s the size,” she whispered. “Smaller things, higher sounds. Bigger things, lower. Just like the caves!”

Ranger Jo’s eyes twinkled. “Pitch. How high or low a sound is. Size makes a difference. That’s why a tiny flute and a big tuba sound so different.”

Excitement like fizzy dew. “If we find different-sized things…”

“We can make different pitches for our parade whistles!” Brim loop-de-looped around her head.

Working with this new understanding, they felt a burst of energy. They searched with fresh eyes and ears. Etta found long hollow reeds from the marsh, as thick as her thumb. Brim, with his sharp eyes, spotted smooth rounded logs that had fallen from an old wise oak. Ranger Jo helped them carefully carve holes of different sizes into the reeds and logs, making sure each one felt just right.

Etta blew into a tiny slender reed. Squeee! A bright cheerful sound. Brim found a thin hollow stick and tapped it with a tiny pebble, and a delicate ting sang out. Etta then blew into a big fat reed, and a strong tooooooot filled the air. Ranger Jo took a wide hollow log and blew across the opening, and a deep resonant bomp echoed through the trees like a happy drum.

Soon they had a whole orchestra of whistles. High squeakers that sounded like happy little birds, medium tooters that sang like friendly trumpets, and deep rumbling bombers that made your tummy feel warm. They arranged them all on a soft patch of moss. When they blew them all together, it wasn’t just noise anymore; it was beautiful music. High whistles danced with low honks, and medium toots wove through them all, creating a sound that was cheerful and grand, absolutely perfect for the Forest Festival parade.

The sun dipped, orange and pink. Ranger Jo gathered them close. Etta held her favourite medium-tooter. Brim let out a happy gentle hoo-hoo, soft as a lullaby. The parade would have controlled sounds that made everyone want to dance.

Tiny reed, high. Bigger reed, low. They packed the orchestra in a basket lined with moss, and Brim rode on the handle, which is bat for first chair.
